analysis.one_liner: Requires credit bureaus to give consumers their credit scores for free, with explanations.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that when consumers get their free annual credit report, they also get a free credit score, along with a plain-language explanation of how the score was calculated and what to do about the factors dragging it down. It would also require companies selling "educational" scores to warn buyers that lenders may use a different score, and would require mortgage, auto, and private student lenders to show borrowers the actual reports and scores used to judge them before they sign the loan. Today, credit bureaus can charge for scores, and the scores sold to consumers often differ from the ones lenders actually use.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers shopping for mortgages, car loans, and private student loans. Anyone who has paid a credit bureau for a score, or been confused by a score that later turned out not to be the one their lender used. The bill also gives extra free reports and scores to people who are unemployed, on public assistance, disputing an error, or victims of fraud and identity theft.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers taking out loans or credit

how_it_helps.text: Requires credit reporting agencies to include a free credit score with each free annual credit report, ending the practice of charging separately for scores.

Requires each score disclosure to list at least four factors that hurt the score and four that helped it, with specific actions the consumer could take to improve it, plus the score range and a graph showing where the consumer stands relative to others.

Requires prominent disclaimers stating that there is no single credit score and that an "educational" score sold to consumers is likely not the score a lender will use, addressing findings from Consumer Financial Protection Bureau reports that consumers' purchased scores often differ from creditor-purchased scores.

Requires mortgage, motor vehicle, and private educational lenders to give borrowers, before signing, free copies of the actual consumer reports and credit scores used in underwriting, with the lender barred from passing on the cost of procuring them.

Automatically provides free reports and scores to consumers who place fraud alerts or security freezes, or who dispute information in their file, and speeds delivery of requested disclosures from 15 days to 3 business days.

analysis.who_pays: The three big nationwide credit bureaus and the companies that sell scores and credit monitoring subscriptions, which lose fee revenue from score sales and face new disclosure duties. Mortgage, auto, and private student lenders must produce and hand over the reports they used, and absorb those costs themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, score sellers, and consumer lenders

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on credit bureaus and lenders, and critics of disclosure mandates argue these costs can be recovered elsewhere in the relationship; the bill itself bars lenders from charging consumers directly for the reports and scores they must now provide.

The bill is a transparency measure, not a fix for the underlying problems: it does not make credit reports more accurate or shorten the time errors stay on a file, so consumers could get clearer views of data that is still wrong.

Detailed formatting mandates, such as 18-point boldface disclaimers and bar graphs with at least six bars, add prescriptive regulatory requirements that some would say go beyond what is needed to inform consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but modest: free scores and clearer disclosures help consumers understand and shop for credit, and the costs are mainly administrative for bureaus and lenders. The main weakness is that it tackles the visibility of credit data rather than its accuracy, so its practical value depends on the underlying reports being right.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the same day in June 2021, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Joyce Beatty, a Democrat from Ohio, introduced the bill on June 23, 2021.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and that was the last action in its history.
The bill had no cosponsors, and no version was ever voted on in either chamber.

The bill's findings cite Consumer Financial Protection Bureau studies from 2011 and 2012 showing that scores sold to consumers often differ from the scores lenders actually use, and a 2015 report finding consumers confused about how to get their reports and scores.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and score sellers keep selling scores that federal law still does not require them to give away, and lenders keep deciding loans on reports borrowers never see before signing.

for.name: Rep. Joyce Beatty
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Free Credit Scores for Consumers Act and made its case in the bill's findings based on federal consumer bureau research.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill; its history ends with the referral.

against.name: Zero House cosponsors
against.what_they_did: No other member signed on during the two-year Congress, leaving the bill without a visible base of support to push it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape is unknown; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: Under current law they must give a free annual report but can charge for a score, and consumer bureau research has found scores sold to consumers can differ from those sold to lenders. The bill would make scores free with the annual report and require explanations, cutting into a fee stream built on that gap.

industries.industry: Credit score and credit monitoring sellers
industries.note: The bill would require prominent warnings that "educational" scores are not what lenders use, and bar calling them credit scores, undermining the marketing of paid score products and monitoring subscriptions.

industries.industry: Mortgage, auto, and private student lenders
industries.note: These lenders would have to hand borrowers, before signing, the actual reports and scores used to underwrite the loan, and absorb the cost of procuring them, making the basis of the lending decision visible at the moment it matters.
